html:
Liess van Halm is a Merganan philosopher and author of The Philosophy of Horror, left unfinished because its author lost his sanity. The book and the philosopher’s own story run through the novel’s middle third: it inspires an exhibition at the Eliste Gallery, attracts Alvaro da Silva’s attention, and ultimately leads him to the castle above Tres Molinos.

Philosophy and reputation

Van Halm was born in Mergana; his surname speaks for itself, but he spoke Catalian fluently. About twenty years earlier, the Academy of Sciences invited him to Laerta. He wrote that horror is a step beyond the edge of the ordered world into chaos, and that all development is such a step. The book and the exhibition’s paintings feature the “Lords of the Abyss” (see Ancients): Ai-Khinar, the Shipbreaker, and Mother-and-Father. The bookseller Jose Flarbo tells Alvaro that ahead of him in sales are the memoirs of Colonel el Cameda, who died in a duel, and van Halm’s book.

Flarbo’s account (ch. 16)

The philosopher lived and wrote on an old estate in Selezia, until he sent away the servants and locked himself in. After some time, an influential man and a doctor broke down his room’s door and found him: the philosopher was emaciated “like a skeleton” and had been eating curtains, book spines, and shoe soles. Flarbo presents this version as common knowledge.

Uncovering the connection with the doctor (ch. 24)

The butler Emil recalls that three months before his death, Juanes received an invitation from the philosopher specifying that he come without companions. He visited and returned displeased: “a very strange man, possibly mental illness.” Three weeks later, a chauffeur with uneven shoulders, sent by Don Maduro, took Juanes away at night, and the following day the doctor wrote in his register: “Liess van Halm, 49, schizophrenia, transferred to the Mercy Clinic.” Beatriz explains that van Halm claimed to have seen the five heroes of Solanta in the Well, a “schönbrun” in Dangarian.

The meeting at the clinic (ch. 26)

For twenty escudos, the orderly Miguel takes Alvaro and Beatriz into a padded room. The philosopher is completely gray-haired, with a mummy-like face and a corpulent body; he constantly chews rice cakes with grass, and when the food is removed, eats chalk and felt. Bite scars mark his left forearm: he has gnawed at himself. He writes something in Merganan, but all Alvaro can make out is meaningless scribbling: the illness has destroyed his ability to write, and the philosopher pounds the wall with his fist in anguish.

Alvaro writes words on the wall. The philosopher shows curiosity at “SCHÖNBRUN” and responds to the names Juanes, Maduro, Deserey, and Fatima the allen: he sniffs and touches the letters, lingering longest over “Juanes.” The name “RODRIGO DA VIRA” draws an intent stare, while “ELIGA. MISFORTUNE” sends him cowering in a corner in terror. Alvaro therefore concludes that the philosopher knew da Vira’s name and fears Eliga.

Miguel tells the story: the philosopher lived near Tres Molinos station, wrote frightening texts for readers, and dismissed his servants. A month or two later, a visiting don found him in the bedroom, where everything had been chewed and his arm was gnawed and tied off with a cord. The door was not locked, and there was food in the cellar, but he would not come out.

Selezia and the House Above (ch. 28–32)

In ch. 28, Beatriz tells Alvaro that van Halm saw the five in the Well and wrote to her mother. In ch. 30, Alvaro concludes that the philosopher found a genuine Well in Selezia and saw the heroes of Solanta in it as living people. In Tres Molinos, they learn that the Merganan moved into the House Above two years earlier and lived as a recluse, sending manuscripts by train. Then he abruptly dismissed the servants, ordered mirrors delivered, and sent out a bundle of letters. A week later, a manufacturer, a noble corsair, a gray-haired gentleman wearing a military bracelet, and a veiled lady visited him; they all left during the night. Later, the same manufacturer returned with a doctor and the tour guide Javier Salam.

In the castle, the philosopher left a study containing portraits of the Lords of the Abyss and drafts of The Philosophy of Horror, breaking off at the same point as the published book. A prison-style hatch has been cut into the bedroom door, the lock merely holds the latch in place, dried filth lies in the corner, and the only new grating is on the window. When Senora Marques warned him about the house’s curse, he replied, “A curse is wonderful! My chance to look beyond the edge of the world.”

Solving the mystery (ch. 34)

Alvaro demonstrates an experiment with the lock for Fernan: a bag of ice on the handle shows that extreme cold thickens the lubricant and jams the mechanism. It was cold on the night immediately after the heroes’ visit; the lock jammed, and the philosopher, believing himself imprisoned, spent a month without paper or a pen. When the thaw came, the lubricant softened, and one turn would have opened the door, but he did not know it. That was how Maduro and Juanes opened it, and van Halm finally lost his reason.

Later, Alvaro develops the theory that Rodrigo da Vira himself came to the castle with his people, seized the philosopher, and forced him to write five invitations to the heroes, whose visit involved drinking the water of “misfortune” (see Dark Schönbrun). Fatima partly confirms this: van Halm wrote the invitations, and what she saw in the Well was not people. She calls the philosopher a true scholar, intelligent and courageous: he looked into the Well voluntarily, wishing to step beyond the world’s boundary and investigate chaos. This is how Fatima understood how the Well of Misfortune works. Alvaro also allows that the philosopher may have drunk the water unknowingly before da Vira arrived.

Who held the philosopher captive (ch. 34)

According to the novel’s ending, the man who seized the castle and forced the philosopher to write invitations was Rodrigo da Vira, also known as Red in the Dangarian chapters. He was not taking revenge on the philosopher himself: Alvaro says that da Vira released him alive and well and bought him ink, paper, and mirrors, while the lock’s snapping shut was not his fault.

Conception and interviews

The available interviews contain no direct comments by the author about van Halm. Speaking of the Ancient gods in general, the author said that in the novel they provide “color” and atmosphere rather than driving the plot; the exhibition of paintings about them was given as an example.

Fate (ch. 34)

At the end of the novel, van Halm remains in the Mercy Clinic. He cannot speak or write; the novel does not show whether his sanity will return.
